newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army says it beat rebels out of hills.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army says it beat rebels out of hills.

text.p: Burundi's army said on Friday it drove Hutu rebels from hills overlooking the capital and aid officials said fighting forced some 30,000 people to flee in the north this month.
The army and main Hutu rebel movement differed on casaulties from three days of violence near the capital and Western analysts expected the rebels would soon return to the heights.
Army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Longin Minani said three soldiers were killed and one wounded before heavy overnight rain ended the fighting on the eastern approaches to Bujumbura.
"It was a successful operation. There were over 100 terrorists killed. We don't know where they are now, but wherever they go we will pursue them," he told Reuters.
Colonel Celestin Ndayisaba, the army commander who directed the operation, said the bodies of nine rebels were found on one hill and the army estimated 100 rebels were killed or wounded.
In Brussels, the Hutu rebel Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) disputed Minani's statement that more than 100 rebels were killed and put the toll at 15 army dead and 11 rebel dead.
FDD spokesman Jerome Ndiho said more than 100 civilians, including women, children and old people, were killed in army raids on the hills but confirmed the rebels had lost some of its positions.
Western analysts expected the rebel force to return to its stronghold in Kibira forest, 25 km (15 miles) to the northeast.
"The army probably won this exchange but it is going to be a pyrrhic victory. The rebels will be back," said one analyst.
Civil war and massacres have killed more than 150,000 people since 1993, provoking fears of a bloodbath similar to Rwanda where up to one million people died in genocide in 1994.
Ndayisaba conceded the army did not have enough troops to secure the hills permanently but said it was recruiting as fast as possible to improve its ability to hold on to territory.

The army used two helicopters and a light plane on Wednesday to strafe and rocket rebel postions on hills at Nyambuye and Gishingano just east of Bujumbura in the first fighting around the capital since the army seized power in a coup on July 25.
Rebels said the attacks were a show of strength against the Tutsi capital hit hard by sanctions imposed by neighbouring states pressing for the military to relinquish power and open peace talks.
New Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya says the rebels must first lay down their arms. The rebels say they will fight on.
Benoit Thiry, acting Burundi director for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP), said up to 30,000 Burundians fled their homes this month because of fighting in the northern province of Kayanza.
He told Reuters the 30,000 were in four camps and WFP was distributing food despite fuel shortages because of sanctions.
The army-appointed Burundian government meanwhile condemned the Hutu-dominated Frodebu party for announcing it was throwing its support to the FDD, saying the move showed they were all "terrorists".
Frodebu was Burundi's largest political party but was banned immediately after the coup. Its leaders have either fled the country or taken refuge in Western embassies in Bujumbura.
